newsitem.title: USA: Negotiator in tobacco talks says deal not imminent.
newsitem.headline: Negotiator in tobacco talks says deal not imminent.

text.p: Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore said Wednesday negotiators in tobacco settlement talks had reached agreement on a laundry list of public health objectives but that no deal is imminent.
"There's no deal imminent," Moore told reporters prior to a conference at a Chicago hotel with public health groups to discuss progress at the months-long negotiations with cigarette manufacturers.
"There's no agreement on the money they'll have to pay. There's no deal on the liability issue. There's no agreement on the nicotine (reduction) issue," Moore said.
However, if the talks do produce a resolution, Moore said the industry had agreed to a comprehensive list of demands, and he anticipated an end to cigarette advertising.

"If we have our way, and I think we will, you won't be seeing any cigarette advertising ... You won't have any 'do smoking' messages in movies" or other types of public promotion of cigarettes, Moore said.
Packages of cigarettes would also display new, presumably stronger, health warnings, he said.

On the list of issues on which there was agreement was a gradual reduction in teen smoking, reaching 30 percent in five years, 50 percent in seven years and 60 percent in 10 years. For every percentage point short of the targets, the industry would pay $80 million -- equal to the profit the industry earns from that number of smokers reaching age 65, Moore said.
In addition, the industry would fund a $500 million "counter-marketing campaign" as well as a "multi-billion-dollar cessation program" that would offer smokers the tools to quit for free, Moore said.
The industry would also accept all proposed Food and Drug Administration regulations governing smoking, he said.
For their part, the states would have to achieve an "85-90 percent" compliance among retailers to limit sales to minors, and would have to withdraw licenses to sell tobacco products from violators.
On the liability issue, Moore said the tobacco industry wanted "absolute and total" immunity from private lawsuits. "They want peace in our time. But they're not going to get it."

He noted that the industry had little to fear from civil lawsuits, since it had won the vast majority of those cases. But the cigarette manufacturers were afraid of the states' pending suits, he said. Those suits by 29 states seek billions of dollars to compensate costs associated with treating smokers' illnesses.
Mississippi, with first crack at the industry, has a trial date set for July 7, and Moore said he had given himself an "artificial" deadline of the next two weeks to reach a settlement in the talks.
"I just hope my lawyers are getting ready for trial. We may be giving opening statements July 7," Moore said. "I'm not sure we're going to get everything we want and if we don't, we'll go to trial.
"They've never faced a group of stalwart attorneys general armed with court dates that can bankrupt the industry," Moore said of the tobacco representatives.

Lonnie Bristow, a former president of the American Medical Association and a participant in the settlement talks, said the major concern of health groups was reducing the number of new smokers who take up the habit.
Other health groups, some not invited to Thursday's consultation set up by the AMA, were more vociferous in their opposition to a deal.
Matthew Myers of the National Centre for Tobacco-Free Kids said he was keeping an open mind.

"If the attorneys general are putting real teeth to that target (of a 50 percent reduction in teen smoking in seven years), then that would be a positive public health change," he said prior to the meeting.
